title: Subdivisions, syncopation, and feel
description: Lock counting grids, syncopation, and straight vs swing.

cards.back: Splitting each beat into equal parts without changing the pulse.

cards.front: How do you count a quarter (the beat itself)?
How do you count eighths against one beat?
How do you count triplets against one beat?
How do you count sixteenths against one beat?
When you switch from eighths to sixteenths, what stays constant?
cards.back: The pulse. Only the grid density (and often the accent pattern) changes.
Accenting weak parts of the beat or bar (the & of 2, beat 4 into 1, etc.) so the rhythm pushes against the expected strong beats.

cards.front: Why does syncopation need a clear pulse underneath?
cards.back: Without a pulse, “offbeat” has nothing to be off. Syncopation is accent against expected strong beats.
Even eighths — both parts of the beat are equal.

cards.front: What is swing feel on eighths?
cards.back: The first of an eighth pair is lengthened and the second is shortened, often near a long–short triplet feel. Harmony does not change.

cards.front: Does switching straight to swing change the chords?
cards.back: No. Feel is weighting of the grid, not a change of chords. Style identity can change instantly on the same pitches.

cards.front: How do you practice syncopation on muted strums for 4 bars?
cards.back: Play eighths but accent only the &s. The pulse stays on 1 2 3 4; the accents sit off the beat.

cards.front: What makes a 1-bar 4/4 eighth pattern syncopated in the exercise sense?
cards.back: It avoids attacking on beat 1 and sits on weak parts of the grid.

cards.front: When you later practice scales or triads, what rhythmic habit should you keep?
cards.back: Assign a subdivision (for example eighths) and keep it honest to the click.
